Jabra Stealth Bluetooth Headset - Black (US Version) I am pleased with this headset; the sound quality is good and audibility is very sharp. The music quality is also good. Assembly is very simple and needs no additional tools to set it together. It also fits well into my ears. I have been using this set for the last three weeks and it works great. It is paired with my cell phone and I use this to listen to the incoming calls and also listen to the music from micro SD card inserted into the cell phone. It is small and has a discreet design. It is very light, easy to carry and works great. The gadget also synchronizes easily with phone, but it does not pair with my Garmin Nuvi GPS machine or my Acer Chromebook both of which are Bluetooth-enabled.

Pairing with cell phone is very easy; just turn the headset on and the cell phone on, it detects the Bluetooth easily and within a minute it gives the message that it is paired. The built-in battery is excellent, and on one charge it lasts for about 5-6 hours of use time. The downside is that this piece doesn't have a separate mute button or the volume button; you have to control volume from your cell phone. Another negative feature is that the three replacement parts for earpiece that comes with the set are of same size, hence gives little option for someone with small (or large) ears. I have rated this product four stars for overall satisfaction.

(Old Model) Seagate 2TB NAS HDD SATA 6Gb/s 64MB Cache 3.5-Inch Internal Bare Drive (ST2000VN000) I've been a fan of Seagate for many years, since their drives are generally long-lasting and reliable, yet inexpensive compared to comparable items on the market. Over the years, I've never had a Seagate hard drive that I felt died too quickly or had any kind of unexpected problem.

So when I was given the opportunity to test this huge Seagate drive, I was thrilled. Obviously, it's a bare hard drive, so you'll need to know how to open up your computer and connect the drive. Once I did that, the drive was immediately recognized by Windows and the drivers installed automatically. In order to make the drive show up and start working in Windows 7, I had to right-click on computer, click manage, double-click storage, double-click disk management, partition it, give it a drive letter, and format it.

This drive is built to handle 24 hour a day use as storage device attached to a network. Because I am a home user, I am not using the full capability of this drive, but for my purposes, having a huge hard drive to store my collection of horticultural images in raw format, this drive is faster than my other (non-solid-state) drive and I'm not noticing any noise when the data is being accessed.

Overall, this is a huge amount of storage space for the price and would make a great drive for home user or small business user. While you'll probably want a superfast solid-state drive to run Windows and other primary programs, I use a regular drive like this for storage on my computer so that I don't need to buy a 3 TB solid-state drive (do they even make those?).
text_fidelity_b: (Old Model) Seagate 2TB NAS HDD SATA 6Gb/s 64MB Cache 3.5-Inch Internal Bare Drive (ST2000VN000)

text_fidelity_a: Bose Wave Radio IV - Platinum Silver I don't know why I didn't notice until I got this.. there is No Way to tune, set alarms..no kind of control EXCEPT on + off unless you use the small remote that is included (button battery).  In my house that means always keeping track of where the remote is and not losing it or the dog eating it.  if something should happen, obviously, you're going to have to contact Bose for another.  On the really positive side..the sound is awesome!  We live up in some hills and are getting great reception.  Bass is adjustable under the settings function and this can be turned up to ear splitting if you wish!  Actually all functions are easy on the remote..  Alarms, snooze, set fav AM/FM stations, time, brightness.  On the FM setting it shows RDS info in text (which can be disabled). RDS shows station, call letters, what song is playing when you're going thru the tuning search. ALSO, has a function where you touch a spot on top to turn unit on/off (can be disabled, cat likes the top!).  NO! Does not have CD player built in! The back has spots for FM external antenna, a BOSE link..input that accepts another Bose linked product, Aux in, 3.5mm stereo headphone jack.  Pricey for a radio/alarm maybe, but, does adapt to aux stuff and sound is really great and unit is sleek looking.  Just don't lose the remote :P

It features Windows 10S operating system that has user-friendly keypad, display and improved sound. The installation is quick and straightforward. This laptop does not include Microsoft Office, but you may purchase from Microsoft Store. This mode is like Windows 10 Home operating system except that you must use Microsoft approved apps from the Microsoft store. In order to run third party apps like Google Chrome, you need to switch out of 10S operating mode to Windows 10 Home. This is a permanent change. Once out of 10S Mode, you can't go back, but you will then have a regular version of Windows 10 Home.

For routine use in S mode, it works well for MS Word, Excel, PowerPoint, internet, social media, emails, printing, etc. This model features 64GB solid state hard drive and works with video games that are compatible with Windows 10 Home 64-bit operating system. The package was delivered on time and the product was intact. I have rated this product four-stars for overall satisfaction.

text_fidelity_a:
D-Link DCS-934L Day & Night Wi-Fi Camera (Black) IP cameras have always been a total pain for me to get up and running. There’s always something that goes wrong, and I end up spending hours getting it to work. This model, however, was a dream to install. The installation quick-start guide is very clear, and offers two options: installing it if you have a D-Link router; or installation with a non-Dlink router. I used the non-Dlink router approach. You download an install program from the Dlink site that walks you through the installation in a clear, easy step-by-step fashion. I had it running in a couple of minutes in hard wired mode, and a couple minutes more to get it to run wirelessly. Very impressed with how easy it was.

The build quality of the camera itself is pretty good. It’s very lightweight but still feels sturdy, and comes with a stand that has a ball and socket joint so you can rotate and position the camera pretty much any way you would need it. The only hardware issue that I didn’t care for was the power cord. It’s rather short (about 4 foot), which limits where I can position the camera. A longer cord – at least 6 foot – would have been a lot nicer.

Using the camera is both easy and frustrating. There is a mobile app, but it’s really only to view the live feed and take snapshots on demand as you watch the live feed. For finer controls and adjustments you need to use a PC and the My D-Link site. That’s where things can be frustrating.

For example, on the settings page there is a clear section dedicated to email notifications with a checkbox. It is strongly implied that checking the checkbox will allow you to receive email notifications after you have set parameters for either motion detection or sound detection. However, after I set parameters for motion detection and then checked the box for email notifications, I did not receive any emails. After doing some searching via Google I found out that I needed to access the "advanced settings" and set up email there too. This was a far more complicated process and required more online research, but after a little bit of trial and error, I got the email notification working. You’ll need info such as the SMTP server address for your email client, the SMTP server port number, and two email addresses for yourself (one for the sender email; the other for the receiver email).

Why a product with such an easy install process has such a complicated usage setup (with much of the info needed not present on the D-Link site) is frustrating.

Once I got the email notification working, I could choose to have it send me an image at the moment of detection, or a set of 6 images (3 images just before detection and 3 images just after detection, at ½ or full second intervals). I can have it always on, or set it to detect only at certain periods of each day. So far I tried the 6 images option and have it always on, and that's worked out reasonably well.

Night vision and day vision seem to work well, with an acceptably clear picture. I have noticed that some times the view remains in night vision mode even when the room is sunny. Not sure why that is happening. Regardless, the picture remains clear.

It cannot record video captured since the camera does not have an SD card option.

You may need to play with the motion sensitivity adjustment and area of sensitivity to get something that works to your preference. I've found that sensitivity definitely needs to be adjusted higher for reliable night views, which means fiddling with the settings each day. While d-link allows you to adjust motion sensors on a day/night basis, it doesn't let you automatically set sensitivity for different times of the day, so that still has to be a manual task.

Although getting some features working is frustrating due to the lack of info on the D-link site, the overall ease of hardware installation, decent build quality, and good picture quality earn this 4 stars. If the D-Link site was improved this would be a five-star camera at this price point.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: D-Link DCS-934L Day & Night Wi-Fi Camera (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White Black Friday sales have brought the Echo Dot to under $30, and that is how I am now buying my second one.

So yes, often times you do need to formulate your requests in a certain way (for instance, try asking Alexa how much time it will take to go to work... I gave up on this...) and enunciate them more clearly if you missed, but in general, this technology is just amazing.
Sometimes I even ask Alexa for information I don't need, just for fun.

I like that they named it Alexa. That's so much better than "Okay Google." It feels like a real person. Who in hell at Google thought it's a good idea to force users to use their company name, and thus remind them that their huge creepy analytics private data gathering network is behind it?

Possible improvements:
* Bring back the matte finish from 1st gen. I shouldn't have to pay more to not have it shiny...
* Listen to the word "stop" when the alarm is ringing. Currently you need to wait until it's not ringing and then say "Alexa, stop."
* Add confirmation and modification prompts to "Add a new event to the calendar." Currently if she misunderstood one word, you have to start all over again.
* Alexa bluntly tells you that she cannot tell you about the events in your calendar on a specific date... C'mon guys...
* Implement the word "Repeat": sometimes you didn't hear or didn't catch the information you were looking for, and currently you have to formulate your request again
* Only gives info about the last Amazon order. She can retrieve more order but you have to be very specific about what they contain.
* I wish Alexa could Google more stuff.
* Choose your own wake up word

I never use Siri on my iPhone, but for some reason it feels very natural to use Alexa, maybe because the device is more "fixed" whereas my phone could be in a backpack, in the other room...

The Killer App is MUSIC. We have an Echo Dot in the bedroom, and my wife just loves to ask Alexa for tunes. We have it linked to Spotify.

Also, I am a software engineer, and I have added some custom features through my own skills. I wish somebody came up with something simple to add your own skills, because this is really useful. For instance, the bus comes in front of my house at the most random times, so I developed a skill that tells me in how many minutes the next buses will come. So much faster than having to check a website on my phone!
text_fidelity_b: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White

text_fidelity_a:
EVOO 14.1” Ultra Thin Laptop FHD, 32GB Storage, 4GB Memory, Micro HDMI, Front Camera, Windows 10 Home I honestly can’t think of an intended user for this laptop. It’s so sluggish that if I gave it to a kid, I can’t imagine them having the patience to wait for the *browser* to open. Let alone go to a website.

I’m a semi-patient adult in my 30s and wanted to chuck this laptop against the wall because the initial setup took so long. For an example, I tried to load the system information to find hardware information, and it took SEVEN seconds to open the Start Menu and load System Information.

The processor is an Intel(R) Celeron(R) CPU N3350 @ 1.10GHz. The laptop has 4GBs of RAM.

My three-year-old phone has 4GB of RAM and is snappier than the EVOO laptop. I have a Chromebook (Acer R11) that is also about three years old, and it’s snappier, too.

Windows 10 S is the default on the laptop, which doesn’t allow you to install any programs not from the Microsoft app store. I suppose that’s useful for basic users, but if you want to put another browser on, you have to disable S mode. Once you disable S mode, you can’t go back to it.

I thought I’d use this laptop for writing, since it’s so slow to load anything that I wouldn’t be tempted to go online. But I don’t even like typing on it; the keyboard feels like I’m typing on a cardboard box. There’s a hollow plastic sound when I type; it’s *that* flimsy. There are some keyboard shortcuts, but I thought it was odd that there wasn’t a shortcut to adjust the brightness. Considering how long it takes the Start Menu to load, that doesn’t make it easy to change the brightness of the screen.

The trackpad is decent, probably the best part of the laptop for me. It has a slightly sandy texture. For an inexpensive laptop, the trackpad isn’t bad.

The laptop is made in China.
text_fidelity_b: EVOO 14.1” Ultra Thin Laptop FHD, 32GB Storage, 4GB Memory, Micro HDMI, Front Camera, Windows 10 Home

Inateck PCI-e to USB 3.0 (4 Ports) PCI Express Card and 15-Pin Power Connector, Red This is a great way to upgrade a PC to USB 3.0 capabilities. Installation is very straightforward – basically just plug the card into a PCI slot, install the included drivers, and you’re done.

I installed this on a Dell Optiplex running Win 7 (32 bit). Totally uneventful, which seems to be a rarity these days with PC upgrades. It actually took me longer to untangle the spaghetti nest of cables and connectors attached to my PC than it did to get the card up and running.

According to the specs it supports XP, Vista, Win 7 and Win 8. There is no support for Mac products at this time.

It has four USB3.0 ports. The port construction is solid, unlike other lower-priced cards I’ve used. Zero wiggling of the port when a cable is attached/removed. It is also downward compatible with USB 2.0 specs – I had no problems using a couple of different USB 2.0 drives on this, in addition to a USB 3.0 drive.

The package included the card itself, a surprisingly well-written, clear install guide, and a variety of power cables to deal with various install options. The drivers come on a full size CD (another plus, since I really hate those mini CDs) and there’s a link in the manual for the manufacturer’s site to get updated drivers.

Absolutely zero complaints about build quality, performance, installation ease, and packaging/documentation. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]

I was skeptical at first, considering the price is much cheaper than any extending arm mount I've seen before. It really is three screws in the wall simple, and allows for fairly easy removal of your TV as well. It even has covers for the screw heads that stay in place without any headaches, all while allowing the whole thing to fold in on itself to give a flat mount. This works out nearly perfect for my in-cabinet storage of the bathroom TV.

Its limitations are that you do absolutely need a stud or masonry to mount this on (which is always true, but since this uses only one vertical line, you are limited to where it can be mounted in case of studs). And also that it does not allow for vertical movement, which some of the very high end models can manage.

The flattest mounts won't extend like this, which is nice for them, but this type will allow you to access your cabling when necessary. Also good for extensions, as in my bathroom cabinet example above.

text_fidelity_a:
CHUWI Hi8 8 inch Windows 10/Android 4.4 Dual Boot Tablet PC, with Features of Intel Quad Core, Full HD 19201200 IPS Screen, 2G RAM/32G ROM and Winkey Price is one thing that's good about this tablet. I have no problem with the cheap plastic all around (really, it almost felt like a disposable food tray), considering the price tag, but there were a couple of things I just couldn't get over.

- Whatever Android OS is installed here, it came without Google Play app. Once I installed it myself, it crashed every time I tried to download a new app from Google app store. This is unacceptable, especially considering that the tablet comes with almost no apps to begin with.
-By the time I updated Windows & set up tablet, it was already getting uncomfortable warm. I can't imagine what would happen if I tried doing something like taping a video for an hour.
- USB socket was loose, I had to jiggle the cable several times to get it charging, and a smallest shift caused it to disconnect again.
- I expected pretty poor camera from the specs, but this was outstanding. Video & images had all the charm and quality of those tiny snapshots from the early mobile phones. Made me kind of nostalgic, but I expect better from a current tablet.

Unrelatedly to the quality of tablet itself, I'm glad I got to try a Windows 10 OS tablet on a dual boot machine, so I know to avoid it from now on... a clumsy hybrid of desktop and tablet capabilities. Android booted and run reasonably fast, while Win 10 lagged on the same machine.

I'm returning it.
text_fidelity_b: CHUWI Hi8 8 inch Windows 10/Android 4.4 Dual Boot Tablet PC, with Features of Intel Quad Core, Full HD 19201200 IPS Screen, 2G RAM/32G ROM and Winkey

text_fidelity_a: AMORNO Bluetooth Headphones, Foldable Wireless Neckband Headset with Retractable Earbuds, Sports Sweatproof Noise Cancelling Stereo Earphones with Mic (Grey) True story.. I go through headphones like they are disposable cups.. Honestly this year alone I have bought 14 pairs of headphones.. both neckband and true wireless ones.. I listen to podcasts all day everyday. I always have a headphone in.. I fall asleep with them listening to Synctuition and I listen to a podcast when I wake up for work. The second I'm out of the shower, an earbud goes in.. I have one pair charging at all times so I'm never without.. Being used heavily.. the bands break, the cords breaks, one bud stops working, one bud goes missing, the Bluetooth stops working, the microphone stops working.. the list goes on.. I probably should just buy an expensive pair but honestly I'm convinced I'll just break or lose them.. So I stick with affordable ones until I inevitably break or lose them.. I tell you this to reassure you that I KNOW my headphones.. These have been great so far. The battery on them is killer. I can get two whole days of literal continuous use before the dreaded "battery low" warning. They retract really quickly and smoothly. They are light weight and the sound is great. I will say though, that I am not qualified to judge sound quality.. I usually only have one bud in at a time to be able to drive, work, talk to others and since it's mostly podcasts.. I can't say that the bass is amazing or the treble is whatever.. I do listen to both at night to sleep music and they sound great but again.. not my forte. Endurance and battery life are though and so far these have far surpassed the usual time when I need to replace them.. Great buy for a great price.
text_fidelity_b: AMORNO Bluetooth Headphones, Foldable Wireless Neckband Headset with Retractable Earbuds, Sports Sweatproof Noise Cancelling Stereo Earphones with Mic (Grey)

text_fidelity_a:
Azio PRISM USB Wired Keyboard with 7 Colorful Backlights, Black (KB507) Overall, this is a decent full-size USB keyboard. The keys are nicely sized and have a medium length throw. There’s little tactile feedback, making the keys feel rather mushy. But, on the plus side, it’s 100% silent in use – no clicky sound of any type.

The layout is a standard QWERTY with a separate number key pad and F1 to F12 at the top. There’s also a separate pad for cursor up/down/right/left.

The back light is very nice and has the unique feature in that you can change the color. There are several to pick from including a “mixed” mode that has several colors making for a rainbow look. Color selection is easy via a dedicated key at the top of the keyboard. Just press it to cycle through the colors. The back light can also be set to off.

The build quality is decent. It’s all plastic and pretty lightweight, but durable enough for normal use. There’s a kick stand on the back that folds out to prop up the keyboard at a comfortable angle, and non-skid feet to hold it in place. I had no problems with this staying put even when banging away at full typing speed. There is some flex in the frame when typing with force, but nothing horrible.

There’s a small area for resting your palm, but it’s rather short to provide much (if any) ergonomic support.

It does not have any indicator lights such as for caps lock, num lock, etc.

Installation is simple on a Win machine -- just a plug-and-play with no drivers needed.

While the overall design is nice and I love the back light feature (plus the ability to change colors), the lack of tactile feel and the lack of status indicator lights drops my rating to 4 stars. Still well worth considering as a replacement full-size USB keyboard, especially if you’re looking for a 100% silent keyboard.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Azio PRISM USB Wired Keyboard with 7 Colorful Backlights, Black (KB507)

text_fidelity_a:
Phaiser BHS-750 Bluetooth Headphones Headset Sport Earphones with Mic and Lifetime Sweatproof Guarantee - Wireless Earbuds for Running, Redheat 3-day update: After trying many tips I'm still not overly impressed. I found I got the best fit with the wire over rear but the mic keeps them from being practical over-ear and the angle of the wire on the other side with the tip at the best angle for kept making the wire come off my ear. In not a fan of comply tips but I finally tried them as a last resort and the sound did improve. But in the end, my theory is that I just can't get these deep enough in my ear due to the large housing to get some bass to balance out the brightness. But even if it did I find the mid-range to lack warmth and certain aspect of the sound to be harsh.

First impression - not as impressed as some

Disclaimer: Everyone's ear is different, and tips make a big difference. Because of my ears, I have to use big tips and a shallow fit. Those who can get a deeper fit my hear something completely different. Also, I'm being really picky to help others decide if this is the right phones for them.

I wanted to try these on my computer because that is where all my music is stored that I've used for decades to audition audio gear. So this will be based on Pandora on my phone at 192kb. This is fine because this is how I will be listening to them.

I could not get a comfortable fit with the included tips. The largest tips were not large enough for my ears. So I dug through my collection and found a good fit. Pairing went fine.

They feel a little heavy to me but maybe that is the price of Bluetooth and the magnets? This is my first pair of Bluetooth in-ears. Build quality seem good for the price (I got them on sale) and I'd say the build quality is about average for their normal selling price. While they look like they have good strain relief it's actually very stiff plastic creating a 'hard point' where the wires come out. I like the little magnet for when I want to take them out but not take them off. It's one of the reasons I got these. If you run, I'd worry a little bit about the weight they add.

The sound. I like tight bass, well controlled, no extra bloom/extension But these are bass shy to my ears. For a workout, I like a fun sound and these ain't that. They are a bit bright and brassy at times I noticed the most on 70s classic rock. They lack a richness in the mids that I noticed most with male vocals. Turning them up did not improve they sound, as they got louder they became painful bright/brassy and bass did not improve. They went loud enough to distort the drivers so volume should not be an issue for anyone.

They do a pretty good job of revealing detail and room acoustics are rendered decently and there is some space around the instruments but not much of a soundstage.

While not sterile they lack some musicality that I'd prefer. Did I mention that male voice sound thin. They lack a fullness and resonance for the male voice. I notice this lack of 'something' on drums as well which are buried in the mix. It seems like the SQ is geared to making them sound impressive and accurate and while they succeed in that to some extent it's at the expense of other parts of the sound. I can see getting some fatigue after a while if you listen for more than an hour or so. Sibilance is not an issue. You hear the sibilance on some songs because it's there but it's not going to wear you out.

I can see why some people would like these especially if you are coming from lower quality mushy sounding earphones. If you are used to better earphones and looking for some less expensive earphones for working out you may like these if you like a 'clear' sound but the word that keeps coming to mind as I listen to them more and more is 'thin'. Not thin/thin but a lack of richness and resonance. If you want some bass especially some extension/bloom (again wearing/tips can make a difference) and a bit of 'drive' I'd consider a different set.
text_fidelity_b: Phaiser BHS-750 Bluetooth Headphones Headset Sport Earphones with Mic and Lifetime Sweatproof Guarantee - Wireless Earbuds for Running, Redheat

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle E-reader, 6" Glare-Free Touchscreen Display, Wi-Fi - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation – 7th) I love reading, but I am consumed by a digital age. I spend so much time playing video games and on social media, I hardly give myself the time to sit down with a good book.

I have a phone, a computer, and a tablet, each with access to the kindle app, but the lights can often cause extreme fatigue when reading for long periods of time.
I could pick up physical copies of books and read those, but often times the font is too small for my bad eyesight, and larger books can be hard to read due to the pages curving.

Enter the Kindle. This ingenious little device fixes every problem I have experienced with digital and physical reading.
Because it does not light up, I do not experience the same fatigue as when reading on my other devices.
I have the ability to increase font size all the way to the point of each letter being about 1/2" tall. The flat design makes it easy to read in any position, I can even put it on a tablet stand and read hands-free!

It is extremely light-weight and does not cause my arms to become tired like large hardcover books do in some positions.

The library of books is incredible! I can read almost any book I want, though there are many that are not yet on the kindle store.

The battery life is phenomenal. I haven't charged it in 2 months and am just now getting a low battery alert! It takes a standard MicroUSB connection.

Over all, this is an excellent device and encourages reading in the digital age.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle E-reader, 6" Glare-Free Touchscreen Display, Wi-Fi - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation – 7th)

text_fidelity_a:
Clip-Case Universal Ergonomic Tablet Stand (Tripod Kit) and Smartphone Mount for iPhone iPad iPod Galaxy Droid Kindle Nook This is one of those "why didn't I think of it?" type products. At first glance, it seems quite simple - basically a mini tripod with attachments that allow you to mount a tablet or phone. But after working with it for a while, it's clear a lot of thought went into this.

The tripod is well made and sturdy, consisting mainly of metal. The ball joint at the top is controlled by a built-in key that allows you to loosen and tighten it so it stays put. Each leg extends independently, so you can set the tripod so it is tilted upward (for example, to position a tablet so you can watch a movie at your desk). The attachment screw base has a rubber non-slip insert to protect whatever you're attaching against scratches. It includes a lanyard, but you can easily remove it (which I did) if it's not needed.

The tripod is very compact -- folds up to about 4.5 inches long and about 1 inch wide, so it's easy to carry. With the legs fully extended it is just under 9 inches tall. The legs have a thick rubber tip that keep it well balanced and positioned. I was a bit concerned that the legs didn't have locks, but the tension of the pull out extensions was more than adequate to keep the legs extended even when it was loaded down with an 8.9 inch Kindle Fire.

Impressive quality given the price - much better than expected.

You can also use the tripod as a camera tripod since the attachment screw is a standard size. It worked fine with my Panasonic and Canon point and shoots.

But the star of the show is the clip. You attach it to the back of the device case (you could attach it to the device itself, but it's not recommended) using an adhesive pad. The pad is removable, but is not reusable, so you want to give some thought before you stick it to the case. Once attached, it fits into a "smart mount" that, in turn, attaches to the tripod. Sounds kind of complicated, but it's very simple to use. There is an included instruction sheet, but you can pretty much puzzle it out by just looking at it.

The clip and smart mount are plastic, but seem more than sturdy enough for the job. They clip together with an interlocking system that kept my Kindle very solidly positioned while I was using it.

The only negative I see is the adhesive pad. As with any adhesive, you need to clean the point of contact very well (an alcohol pad is included in the box) and let the adhesive cure for 30 min. I think it's a safe bet that some people won't do both those steps, which opens the door to a significant point of failure.

But, provided you read the instructions, this is a very nicely designed and useful product. Highly recommend.
[The manufacturer provided the product for review]
text_fidelity_b: Clip-Case Universal Ergonomic Tablet Stand (Tripod Kit) and Smartphone Mount for iPhone iPad iPod Galaxy Droid Kindle Nook

Legrand - Wiremold Cable Management Kit, Cord Organizer and Hider, Concealer, C210S Cord Cover Kit, White I'm sure they do it for shipping purposes and to appeal to homeowners without tools, but I don't like that they give you multiple short pieces instead of fewer long pieces that you could cut down to appropriate size. That just means you need more couplers; each additional coupler decreases the appeal of the final installation.

Honestly, I hate surface mounted conduit. But there are times when it is required, and in those cases better than nothing. I own my home, so of course I put all permanent links properly inside the walls, but even then, there are times when the Cat/RG/other jacks are not directly behind the furniture holding the devices that need the cables. In these cases, I prefer to mount these with screws, and then caulk and paint them into the painted baseboards so they blend in better, although they have made these with tape for truly temporary installations.

There is just one connector for an inside corner and an outside corner (on the x/z axis). And in my opinion, these are the only two you should really need, and you probably need more of them. I am never going vertical up walls with cables; I just go from the jack along the baseboard to behind the furniture...if I need more than that, I'm afraid I need to just stop being lazy and tear down a wall or something.

I get that if you are in an apartment or a rental property, you may need more flexibility with this. But in my opinion, if you can't do a proper wall-mount TV install without surface-mount conduit, then you should just use a TV stand as God intended because this is not enough to make cables acceptable in such an install (although honestly, it is better than nothing).
text_fidelity_b: Legrand - Wiremold Cable Management Kit, Cord Organizer and Hider, Concealer, C210S Cord Cover Kit, White

Dell Venue 7 16 GB Tablet (Android) This is a great tablet for the money. It is sturdy, lightweight, and easy to use.

The tablet has a good weight for its size. It featues a 7 inch screen, the back of the devise smooth matte black with the Dell logo on it.

The power button is on the top right, Volume rocker buttons are on the left along with the micro USB port (used for charging with the included charger or for connecting to your computer) The right has an expansion slot for a micro SD card.

It runs Android 4.2.2. If you are at all familiar with Android this will be a snap. I have a Samsung Galaxy and they are pretty much identical in the way they operate. Only difference is the slight additions that Samsung adds to their phone operating system user interface. The system is pretty clear of bloatware, so there are very few apps that usually come preloaded on your phones.

Setup is easy. Answer a few questions and you are off and running. If you have a google account (gmail, google plus) you enter that and you can begin downloading apps you've previously downloaded on our phone or purchased.

The system runs very smooth and fast. It boots in under 30 seconds. Switching screens, loading apps, and opening menus is blazingly fast. It is really really fast.

The screen is very bright and can be viewed at some intense angles and it looks very good.

The front facing camera is decent, though not excellent. It comes in at about 3 megapixels, pretty good for taking photos. They are a bit grainy, though passable. Definable will not replace your regular camera. The rear facing camera is not good at all, you will not be taking very good selfies with this. It is passable, though, for doing things like Skype or participating in a Google hangout or video conference it will do a good job because you usually don't want to broadcast on too high a resolution anyway.

Most any google apps will run on this. I've seen no problems or incompatible apps. I've used Netflix, Hula, Pandora, and others. They load fast and multimedia looks good.

This does not run flash! So if you want to view sits like Amazon streaming movies you will have a hard time. I am looking for a workaround, but as of writing this have not found one.

The sound quality is very good. the speakers are on the bottom and they sound pretty good. There is a headphone/data port on the top. So you can listen to music with headphones or use an input device such as a credit card reader like I have with the Square Register app or with headphone/microphone devices.

Battery life is good. If you are using it hard, you'll have to charge it every evening, though if you use it here and there, you can get a few days out of it.

It also has Bluetooth connectivity and it has worked well connecting to my various devices. Wireless is fast and easy to set up

The only weird thing is the micro USB cord seems to be upside down. That is though the plug fits in snugly to the device, it seems contrary to what you expect. I'm always trying to put the USB connector in upside down. Just kind of funny and does not diminish the device.

Overall a sturdy capable tablet. Runs very fast, good battery life, clear screen, and good sound. Will run most any app you'd care to run. If you are familiar with Android, you'll have no problems using this and it'll seem like old hat. Very easy to learn, setup, and use.

I highly recommend!!

UPDATE!!:: As of December 19th, 2013 there is an OS upgrade. This now runs Android 4.3. If you have this already and it is NOT running 4.3, go to Settings/About Tablet/system updates
text_fidelity_b: Dell Venue 7 16 GB Tablet (Android)

text_fidelity_a:
Winegard HD8200U Platinum VHF/UHF HDTV Antenna (65 Miles+, Digital, 4K Ultra High-Def Ready) First, be aware this beast is more than 14 feet long and about 9 feet wide when unfolded and assembled. It does move in the wind. It doesn't weigh that much, but with so many elements forming such a large device it becomes a sail.

I mounted it on a 10' length of 1-1/4" electrical conduit held to a tall garage wall using [[ASIN:B001RCMEEA Channel Master CM-9025 3-Inch Heavy-Duty Wall Mount for TV Antenna Masts]]. The antenna is about 23 feet in the air.

The HD8200U has a very high-gain, directional Yagi UHF antenna on the front and a full VHF antenna on the rear. I really don't think I need the VHF section and may retire this antenna and opt for a more compact UHF Yagi if the high winds we occasionally experience cause trouble. After assembly, the two sections feed into an electronics box using 1/8" aluminum rods from each section. You then mechanically attach a top plate to the box that connects to all four aluminum leads. The coax connector is in this top plate. A weather boot is supplied to seal the connection.

The HD8200U does bring in the signal like a champ. My stations are at least 19 miles and 68 miles away. It's very directional. If I aimed 30 degrees off, I got zero channels. Check where your stations are broadcast from using www.antennaweb.org (antennaweb dot org) which provides distance and direction in degrees from magnetic north using your zip code. Very handy.
text_fidelity_b: Winegard HD8200U Platinum VHF/UHF HDTV Antenna (65 Miles+, Digital, 4K Ultra High-Def Ready)

Foldable Bluetooth Keyboard, Geyes Folding Wireless Keyboard with Portable Pocket Size, Aluminum Alloy Housing, Carrying Pouch, for iPad, iPhone, and More Tablets, Laptops and Smartphones(Gold) This folding keyboard is a bit of a betwixt and between product, but if it is the sort of thing you think you might use, then it’s got a lot to like about it. If you have a tablet (and my experience is with iPads so keep that in mind), then their built in keyboard is a better choice for short work just because it’s larger and more natural to type. For longer work, the choice will be more individual in that some people hate writing for extended time on the hard surface of a tablet keyboard and others don’t mind at all. I can do a pretty long stint and for really long work, I’ll shift over to a Bluetooth keyboard, either Apple’s own or a smaller Logitech one that also acts as a cover. I’d prefer both of those to this because again, they are larger and so more comfortable.

When one considers the keyboard as a phone accessory, then things change a bit, and this become a much more viable choice. If I have to do any halfway extensive typing on a phone for work (something beyond texting, an email or two, etc., then this would definitely be my preference over the phone itself.

1) it takes up very little space (and comes with a nice little pouch). Tossing it into a backpack is nothing, but I could easily fit it into a coat pocket, a cargo pants-like pocket, keep it in my car console without it blocking much space. None of which would be true for my wireless Apple keyboard or even my slimmer Logitech one. The additional “bulk” is therefore relatively negligible.

2) the typing is quite nice on it. I was pleasantly surprised at the key travel, the ease, the tactile sense.

3) It’s definitely small and a little cramped, but not so I notice it unless I’m typing for a long time (half hour or more) and then I just need to take a few minutes break. The small size doesn’t come into play too often. I had to readjust to the apostrophe, and one has to hunt and seek a bit for less-used keys, but that’s easy enough and once you’ve been typing for a while it becomes just as second nature as normal typing does. And it’s much faster and much more comfortable than extensive phone typing

4) the stand is a nice little touch that works quite well, placing the phone at a usable and pleasant working angle and letting you sue it in both portrait and landscape mode.

5) I haven’t exhausted the battery so can’t speak to how long it will go, but it’s certainly lasted a good number of hours, more than I’d ever use it for (if I’m working that long I’m going to my laptop or tablet)

6). Build quality seems sufficient. I wouldn’t say it feels highly durable, but nor would I call it cheap feeling or overly flimsy. And when it’s folded I have no concerns about it breaking.

All in all this was actually quite the pleasant surprise and again, if you would ever find yourself needing to use your phone for that sort of mid-range work (more than you’d want to do on a phone keyboard but not so much you’re turning to a laptop) then I’d highly recommend it.
text_fidelity_b: Foldable Bluetooth Keyboard, Geyes Folding Wireless Keyboard with Portable Pocket Size, Aluminum Alloy Housing, Carrying Pouch, for iPad, iPhone, and More Tablets, Laptops and Smartphones(Gold)

Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors) The Lexar jump drive was the speediest drive I have, but it does feel a little more cheaply made than some. Some specifics:

I used a Macbook Pro, mid 2012
I copied over a folder with 3000 items in it, a mix of file types including video, photos, presentations, docs, PDFs, Final Draft, spreadsheets
This Lexar copied the files over in just under 5 minutes
An older Lexar USB 3.0 took exactly 8 minutes
A Transcend 3.0 took about 8.5 minutes
A Sandisk 2.0 took much longer. In the same time this Lexar took to fully copy the folder, the 2.0 Sandisk was less than a third of the way through

I did a bit more copying of fewer files and the results were consistent--this one was faster on a regular basis

Formatting for my Mac was fast and simple.

It comes with a 2-inch lanyard to attach to a key chain or whatever.

My single concern is build quality. It is plastic, like most of my flash drives, but it feels less sturdy, a bit more cheaply made. And it seems particularly thin at the outlet end (where the USB prong exits). If it breaks I'll update.

So far then, the speed is a definite plus. It's the fastest of my 3.0 flash drives. And certainly anyone with a 2.0 will want to upgrade--the difference, assuming you can take advantage of it, is hugely significant. Just that build quality to be worried about, but so far so good

text_fidelity_a:
Pixel Mago Canon Speedlite ETTL High Speed 5D2 5D3 6D 7D 60D External Speedlite While this flash doesn’t outperform the Canon Speedlite, it comes the closest of any of the Speedlite “clones” I’ve tried so far, and does so with impressive build quality.

I was impressed with this right out of the box mainly due to the care taken with packaging. No, packaging doesn’t impact the performance of the flash, but it does take the worry out of getting one that is damaged due to UPS handling. The flash is packed in a carry case (which is very well-made and has cushioning) and, in turn, packed inside of an air-filled tube case. Together they provide more than ample protection against transit-born bruises short of being run over by the UPS truck.

The flash feels very solid. The head articulates up/down/left/right and has indents at the most commonly used angles. The head is a bit stiff to move, but I consider that as a positive since I don’t want the head getting bumped out of place when I have it positioned the way I want it.

The hotshoe frame is plastic but feels very solid. There’s a rotating locking ring to keep it in place while on the camera. It made contact and worked just fine on a 5D Mark II, a 4D and a Rebel.

The battery compartment door has a spring-loaded hinge so it pops up when unlatched. Again, good build quality on that (which is a common point of failure on other low-cost flashes I’ve used). It uses 4 AA batteries. It ran fine on rechargeables.

The control panel and LCD screen are both easy to use and see for the most part. The buttons beep when pressed, but that can be turned off if you want a silent operation. Some of the icons on the screen are very small – I needed to squint a bit to make some of them out. Then again, my aging eyes could be a contributing factor.

Most of the commands are executed by pressing a button and then selecting options using a rotating wheel. The wheel is the only part that didn’t work all that well at times. Sometimes a single twist moved it through the menu; other times I needed to twist it a couple of times to get it to register.

The capabilities of this flash are very impressive given the price point. It offers synch flash, manual flash, curtain synch, up to 1/8000 second synch, master/slave mode, AF assist beam, TTL flash, zoom settings and an LED lamp. It also has a nice amount of convenience features such as auto off (with various timed settings ranging from 5 minutes to 2 hours), a lock mode, screen on/off and test mode. It even has a USB port that can be used to update the firmware should updates be available (at this writing I am not aware of any updates).

The manual is not great. It offers a decent listing of the capabilities, but is often sparse in pointing out the details. But, if you have some measure of experience with a flash, it’s not hard to figure out (with a bit of experimenting) how to use it.

Given the price, this is an excellent value. It probably won’t suit the needs of a professional photographer but for an amateur (even a very avid one) it’s an excellent alternative to Canon gear at a much nicer price.
text_fidelity_b: Pixel Mago Canon Speedlite ETTL High Speed 5D2 5D3 6D 7D 60D External Speedlite

text_fidelity_a:
Konnek Stein True Wireless Earbuds, Bluetooth 5.1 Active Noise Cancelling Headphones, Sliding Design Charging Case 500mAh, IPX4 Waterproof, Deep Bass Built-in Mic Call for Business & Sports - Black The KONNEK STEIN True Wireless Earbuds are a decent set of wireless earbuds. The sound quality is good, I’ve been using them with music and streaming shows, and I haven’t been disappointed with the sound quality.

I’m not as pleased with the short battery life, touch controls, and lack of audio cues.

I get about 2-3 hours of playback per charge. It’s rare for me to battery drain earbuds, but with this pair, I hear the low battery chime every time I use them.

The touch controls and lack of audio cues go together. The touch controls are super easy to activate on accident. More than once I’ve taken the earbuds out only to find I hit Play while doing so, and they kept playing music. I also activate random controls when adjusting the earbuds in my ears … and I don’t always know what I’ve done. Did I turn ANC on or off? The audio cues are just beeps, not an announcement like “ANC on/ANC off.”

I like the design of the case. It has a sliding top, so you can actually clean the entire area where the earbuds sit. When you put the earbuds inside the case, a light flashes to show their battery level. The case charges wirelessly or via USB-C. There’s only one LED light on the outside of the case, it’s easy to miss when you’re trying to see if the case is charging or not.
text_fidelity_b: Konnek Stein True Wireless Earbuds, Bluetooth 5.1 Active Noise Cancelling Headphones, Sliding Design Charging Case 500mAh, IPX4 Waterproof, Deep Bass Built-in Mic Call for Business & Sports - Black

The car had a 11 speaker dolby surround sound system with factor CD player and factory 6 CD changer. The cable that came with the Grom device was adequate but cheap. Within 4 months the cable's outer casing had separated from the jack portion and exposed wire occurred. Even with electrical tape to prolong the inevitable, the loud feedback issues got worse. I finally ordered this and am very happy with it. It fits despite my protective case for my Note8. Audio quality is perfect. I am hoping the braided type cord will stand up to use better. The cable passes through a small hole I drilled in the back of the storage slot built into the stereo, feeds back to the small Grom device which I heavily electrical taped in place so it doesn't get unhooked and force me to tear the stereo out again. I shoved all but about a foot of the cable back behind the stereo and it passes smoothly through the hole as needed but my phone rarely leaves the Spigen magentic vent phone holder in my car.

10/15/18: docked 2 stars- cable stopped working- threw off horrid feedback and couldn't stand using to listen to my phone in my car after barely 6 months. It was never kinked, damaged, or abused, it was kept tied in loose loop and simply plugged into and removed from my phone 1-3 x a day. No reason for it to stop working. Trying an Anker brand cable and if it can't last at least a year I'm done with aux cables, I'll upgrade to Grom bluetooth.

This display produces beautiful and accurate colors once you turn down the brightness significantly, which I set to 30. The contrast is good but nothing to write home about.

I use this primarily for gaming, so the first thing I did was enable GSync from nvidia control panel, and set a framerate limiter of 72 using rivatuner (3 less than the 75hz refresh rate of the monitor, as is recommended). And I am really impressed, motion is fluid and responsive like I've never seen before as I'm coming from a 60hz TN panel, significantly better than just Vsync on that. Works perfectly on every game I've tried on it, including Far Cry 5, GTA, Modern Warfare, The Witcher 3, Shadow of the Tomb Raider, FIFA etc. I would have gone for a 144hz display but given the capabilities of my 1070ti for the games I play, 75hz seemed like the sweet spot for me. Highly recommended

Original review* DOA. Worked for 10 mins or so, then simply turned off while I was tweaking picture settings on its OSD. Tried swapping the power cable, flipped the switch and waited a few seconds but nothing, no power indicator light at all.

text_fidelity_a:
Roku N1100 HD Media Player (Old Model) I've been researching ways to increase my cable channel happiness and reduce the costs. My research started a while ago, but a Cosumerist post about subscriber fees really got my goat. Look at all the junk channels that we are forced to pay for. I could care less about any sports channel or 90% of everything else. It is my opinion that we should be able to choose extra channels separately after we hook up with basic cable. You'll also notice that BH charges extra for a special HD tier. Sure it's only $6 a month, but geez, look how much markup there is. Anyways, you get the idea. I don't have any issues with BH. They've served me well for a few years. But I need more of what I want. Not what BH thinks I want.

So, I dropped down to basic cable and purchased a Roku HD unit. Set-up was a snap. I used HDMI for the TV and stream with a N router.

OMFG! This thing is amazing! In short, it streams unlimited Netflix offerings to your TV. The cheapest Netflix subscription ($9) is all you need. Plus it streams Amazon Video On Demand, and a bunch of internet channels. You can stream wirelessly or hard wire with an ethernet cable.

Can you tell I'm excited? Anytime I can boost my entertainment for less dollars is always a good day. The Roku will pay for itself in 2 months after switching to basic. And its HD!

Sigh...I must go.

I've been watching the original Dr. Who from the 60's.
text_fidelity_b: Roku N1100 HD Media Player (Old Model)

Usage is about as easy as can be: one dial for frequency; one dial for volume (and on/off). There's a tone switch that basically enhances the bass (it sounds much better with bass enhancement). It can switch between AM, FM and shortwave. FM reception is excellent. I could not, however, get anything other than static on the SW band (probably due to where I am located rather than the radio itself). It can run on batteries (not included) or an AC adapter (which is included).

The build quality is just OK. It doesn't have much of a solid feel to it, and is lightweight. This is not a radio you can toss around and expect it to make it through in good shape.

A great item to have on hand when the power goes out (provided you remember to stock up on batteries) or just to be able to listen to the radio without the Internet. Five stars.

text_fidelity_a:
Tile - (Gen 1) - 1 Pack - Discontinued by Manufacturer The Tile system isn't perfect but it works (mostly) and to date I haven't run across any better options. So bearing in mind your needs and the device's limitations, it's probably worth getting (at the time of this writing) if you have things you're worried about misplacing.

Pros:

- EASY setup. The time it takes to send an eMail and receive a reply, and a few seconds more. I have heard people say it requires iPhone 4 and up - I have a 5 and everything was a breeze. I didn't use the picture feature initially but it was no problem to update later.

- Decent map feature - good enough to get you in general range of the FIND radius.

- An audible FIND jingle. Just loud enough to hear through a wallet. Louder sure would be better, but it has a tinny high-pitched jingle that's easy to identify once you've heard it.

- It's small enough to fit in my wallet. It's a bit bulky, but it does.

- It's weatherproof and sealed. I haven't actually tested that and don't want to, but it's a nice feature.

- On-phone settings are easy to operate, and allow you to turn off Bluetooth tracking without turning off the iPhone's Bluetooth.

- Easy to assign to other objects as needed (if you don't use the stick pad.) It has a hole, so you don't HAVE to stick it to anything permanently.

- Can add other users (beforehand, of course!)

- It works. The battery is only supposed to last about a year, though (we'll see!)

Cons:

- Bulkier than I thought - not quite as thick as a pen, but almost. About a half-dollar size.

- The FIND process takes a minute or two to adjust and is a little confusing at first.

- The FIND radius sure isn't perfectly accurate. But hey, it's something!

- Battery not replaceable. The Tile people will recycle it for you for a fee, but I doubt that is a rapid process.

I really like it. I don't lose stuff that often, but this is an awfully convenient tracking option - having a general idea is a LOT better than having NO idea at all! And I LOVE the idea of the Tile community! The Tile gives me peace of mind taking things through airports etc. If there's something you think you MIGHT mislay, I think the Tile is worth it.
text_fidelity_b: Tile - (Gen 1) - 1 Pack - Discontinued by Manufacturer

TRAM 7732 Satellite Radio Low-Profile Mirror-Mount Antenna [[VIDEOID:cbe7b798430f2aea6c124b1ed1015e2]] My husband has wanted a new antenna for his truck for quite some time. We had one with a long antenna in our wishlist for a year or more. We have, I would say, a middle class income, and only my husband works. We keep a pretty tight budget and sometimes needs and wants get weighed heavily.

The antenna he had finally started to really not work well and as I was going to purchase it (it would have been $22) he asked me to look for the low profile version. The low profile version, THIS version, ended up being $35, so more money. Presently, this antenna has been worth the money and made my husband VERY happy. He runs local and is home every night, but still, 16 hours a day in a truck, I want him to be happy. His Sirius radio makes him happy.

He installed this in about 15 minutes and the cabling goes in through a small waterproof port above his window that was already there. He drives a pneumatic bulk tanker daycab. The connection to his mirror is very secure. It is not a big ole antenna that says HERE I AM. It is very subdued.

text_fidelity_a:
Final E3000 in-Ear Headphones, Hi-Fi Sound Quality, Hires Certified, Award Winning, Stainless Steel Housing, 3.5mm Standard Plug, Natural Sound with Extended Bass, Designed in Japan I am not shy about returning headphones I don't like but these are KEEPERS. This might be the happiest I've been with some earphones since my beloved Nuforce NE-700X. But to be fair those cost $90 in 2014.

Update after 2 weeks of use:

I went to a larger tip and now they don't sit as far in my ear. The bass and soundstage both improved with more air around the instruments. I really like these. I don't find myself thinking oh they do this, or they don't do that with regard to sound. The just play the music. That little TINY bit of graininess is gone with some break in I guess. While I don't listen to Metal or EDM they handle all genres of music well and handle more complex music like rock well compared to others I have tried. They come with 4 size tips so finding the right size is easier compared to pairs that only come with 3 size tips. The tips grip the nozzle really well but still come off and go on pretty easily. They come with some really small ear hooks but I haven't tried them yet. There is no listening fatigue yet they are still pretty accurate. They do not go really loud but they do go loud enough for me.I haven't played with EQ much because I haven't felt the need. Wires are thin and tangle pretty easily and don't untangle very easily. I have not noticed any microphonics. Of course, I'd like to have $100 buds but for $55 dollars they hit my nice but I won't cry if I lose them price point.

===========================================
Original review

They are not even broken in yet (and they don't need it) but my only real complaint and it's nitpicky, but they have a touch of graininess. But nowhere near as much as the Carbo Tenor. These are very neutra with decent detail while never being too bright. There is nice seperation between instruments but not much of a soundstage but there is nice amount of 'air' around the intruments. They do not have a lot of extension but they are not bass shy like the Carbo Tenor were. Drums sound natural, again not like the Carbo Tenor where they sounded more like carboard boxes.

They are very light so they very comfortable. (I like straight earphones the best) The default tips fit me the best which is a nice change for me. There is next to no strain relief on the earphones as you can see in the picture so if you are hard on headphones, maybe consider other phones. on the good side the lack of strain relief makes them very comfortable worn wire up which i want for the gym. They have vents on the back so I doubt that isolation is very good for in-ear phones.

In summary these are nuetral sounding with out any of the 'problems' of hifi. They are never over sibilant and they do not punish badly recorded songs or when listening to low bit rate stuff like pandora. I would call them fun for working out but they are not too dry if the quality of the music is what you want. They are not going to impress anyone or give you an eargasm when listening to your best music. But at $54 I'm extemely please with them and for me are a big step up from the Carbo Tenor unless you are impressed by a forward/blaring sound.
text_fidelity_b: Final E3000 in-Ear Headphones, Hi-Fi Sound Quality, Hires Certified, Award Winning, Stainless Steel Housing, 3.5mm Standard Plug, Natural Sound with Extended Bass, Designed in Japan

text_fidelity_a:
Jaybird Freedom Sprint Bluetooth Headphones - Retail Packaging - Midnight Black Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. They are my first pair of bluetooth buds and it has been wonderful to not have to deal with cords, especially when working out. I can't tell you how many times I've hit an earbud cord while exercising and ripped the ear bud from my ear. A real pain in the neck (and ear!).

>>>Pros:

Comfort - These fit very well in my ear. There are different tip sizes to create a good fit and, after trying them all out, I went with the medium size. Very comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

Stay put - I've yet to have them fall out even when doing aerobic exercises or while on the treadmill.

Sound - they sound pretty good. The sound is not as good as my favorite (and inexpensive) corded buds ([[ASIN:B0053R0WWG RHA MA-350 Aluminium Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones]]) but they are a solid B+ performer with regard to bass response and overall clarity. Keep in mind that good bass response is affected by how the buds fit in your ear, so it's important to try out different tip sizes to see how they affect sound quality. They do get harsh at loud volumes, but for normal listening they are more than fine for my non-audiophile ears. They do reasonably well at blocking out ambient noise.

Setup - I found it straightforward even though I've never had any experience with setting up bluetooth earbuds.

Size - nice and compact so you don't get the "radar dish" look that larger units can have.

Durability - they have a "sweat proof" guarantee which is nice (although I imagine, like most guarantees, there are some loopholes). Overall build quality is good, with a very solid feel to all components.

>>>Cons:

Battery life - The manufacturer claims a battery life of 4.5 hours but I've yet to get more than 3 hours off a single charge. Plus there's no warning about battery life (until you're almost fully discharged) or a visual indicator of how much charge there is left.

Usability - the buttons on the buds are too small, making it difficult for me to push the right one. A lot of fumbling and mis-presses, making it often easier to deal with volume changes on the device, which kills some of the value of having wireless buds. I guess I lack the nimble fingers of the primary target market.

But overall, I'm pleased. The pros outweigh the cons, and I think this is a solid 4-star device.
text_fidelity_b: Jaybird Freedom Sprint Bluetooth Headphones - Retail Packaging - Midnight Black

There are workarounds to get some google play stuff to work without rooting, but not paid apps and not in game purchases. You can't link your Fire to the googleplay store so if it's your only device, you're out of luck.

Fire would be the best all around tablet, if amazon and google play would learn to play nicely with each other and share. Still, I highly recommend Fire HDX

SABRE Home Security Personal Safety Kit, Comes With A 120 dB Doorstop Alarm, 120 dB Door Or Window Alarm And A 120 dB Personal Alarm, Safety Essentials For College Students, Home Owners and Travelers With crime rates going up in NYC, this is an ideal kit for anyone living in an apartment, especially if they're alone and elderly. It covers two areas most vulnerable to thieves: your window and the door, while the key chain is best for when you're coming home late at night on a dark, lonely street. Just pull the pin and the alarm screams.

Of the three items, I would say the window alarm rates highest in terms of usefulness. In fact, I wish this set came with three of them. We travel a lot, and the biggest fear we have is intruders breaking in through our high-rise window, as we have a fire escape near one of them.

The door stop is the least useful to me as a thief would have to break through one of our windows first before going through a door. My front door is already secured by locks and the other doors in our place generally remain open. I suppose we could reinforce the front door with the doorstop, but it seems like overkill. If you lived in a dorm and wanted a particular room to be off-limits, I suppose it would be useful in that case. This item reminds me of the alarm that would be set off if you used an emergency exit. As if in acknowledgement that this item won't be used as much as the others, no battery was supplied for it, unlike the others.

As for the key chain, this is one of those devices that will lay dormant for long periods (knock on wood). You'll have to remember to check and test the batteries occasionally because it will be rarely used.

Overall, for the price this set can't be beat. It feels more like a "sampler" pack, though, as it has only one of each product when multiples of each one would have been more helpful.
text_fidelity_b: SABRE Home Security Personal Safety Kit, Comes With A 120 dB Doorstop Alarm, 120 dB Door Or Window Alarm And A 120 dB Personal Alarm, Safety Essentials For College Students, Home Owners and Travelers

Compact size is great for travel, since older hotels don't have enough power outlets for modern travelers and the outlets are often hidden behind desks or under beds.

Unfortunately, the USB power ports are pretty weak. You get 2.4A divided among 3 ports, so if you're trying to charge 3 devices, each one gets less than 1A. Modern smartphones and tablets will often fast-charge at 3A, so charging with these ports will be very slow. USB powered laptops can use even more power and will complain about being charged at less than 3A.

I don't like that there is no USB-C charging port and no USB Power Delivery fast charging, which are becoming the standard for smartphones and laptops.

This device is not UL listed for electrical safety. As phone and tablet and laptop batteries get more and more powerful, electrical safety becomes more and more important. Most power strips from US brands are UL listed, so I cannot recommend a product that is not UL listed.

For someone who hasn't had a pair of "real" headphones since the early 80's, I was a little skeptical about the weight on my head, the quality of the sound, and the flexibility of something other than my earbuds. What a wonderful revelation. These headphones are extremely lightweight (in fact I wore them for about 2 hours straight and forgot I had them on when I was getting ready to leave the house), the cord that connects to your device is a very comfortable 48 inches long, they are flexible enough to conveniently fold down and place inside of a small pouch which is included, and as for the sound - it is simply incredible.

The ability to have the Jabra App convert most of my songs into an upgraded Dolby Digital Plus format at no additional cost is the real deal clincher. The music is breathtaking and made me wonder how I ever enjoyed the songs before these came along. Now I carry the little pouch in my purse and take them everywhere.

All I can say in conclusion is that if you really love your music and want to appreciate it at the highest level, for the price these are a wonderful investment. Save the earbuds for the gym, and use these headphones when you truly want to feel the music.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra REVO Corded Stereo Headphones - Retail Packaging - Gray (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

Lenovo Legion Y720 Gaming Laptop, 15.6" Full HD, Intel Core i7-7700HQ Processor, 16GB DDR4 RAM, 512GB SSD, GeForce GTX 1060-6GB, Windows 10 Signature Image - 80VR0078US Like all dedicated gaming laptops, this is a big heavy high-powered machine. It is portable enough to lug over to your buddy's house for play dates, but it is too bulky and heavy to carry to work everyday. Construction is very good with an aggressive-looking aluminum case to match the aggressive-sounding "Legion" product name. Mechanical keyboard has decent (but not the best) travel and the large keys are backlit so you can easily play your games in the dark. Dolby Atmos audio works well for games, but is kind of thin for music or movies unless you hook it up to external speakers. This Y720 version has a 1080p IPS display, which is OK but not as bright or contrasty as some other laptops I have used. There is also a more expensive 4K display available, but I have not tried that.

Core i7 CPU with 16GB of RAm gives you really great performance. This machine is easily powerful enough for any games I tried on it. Even though performance is throttled somewhat when run off the battery, battery life is still less than 2 hours under heavy use (maybe 6 hours with light use).

For the money, it is hard to go wrong with these Lenovo Legions. If you don't want to spend more than $1000, the cheaper Legion Y520 is almost as good for most types of games and costs $300 less.
text_fidelity_b: Lenovo Legion Y720 Gaming Laptop, 15.6" Full HD, Intel Core i7-7700HQ Processor, 16GB DDR4 RAM, 512GB SSD, GeForce GTX 1060-6GB, Windows 10 Signature Image - 80VR0078US

Sandisk has done a poor job of clearly communicating this, but it is in the description.

These values are highly variable. These little things are great for data transfer and off-line storage. Do not use them to replace a high-speed hard disk. If you need that, you'll need to get something like a UHS-II V90 SD card with an appropriate UHS-II reader. Or, like, you know, an actual hard disk?

text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR Nighthawk 4-Stream AX4 Wi-fi 6 Router (RAX40) – AX3000 Wireless Speed (Up to 3 Gbps) | 1,500 Sq Ft Coverage Bought this router a few days ago and have already begun the return process. I didn't have a good gut feeling about this router from the start, partly because the reviews are not all raves and partly simply because it looks kind of...evil to me. I am definitely not a fan of the hyper-aggressive router design trend that seems to be targeted at adolescent male gamers. I do not look at this thing and think it looks cool and feel positive feelings; I look at it and feel...apprehension. As a physical object, it's not something I really want in my apartment. But I decided to give it a try anyway because I don't think that kind of gut feeling should be one's primary consideration in choosing a router, and because I often like having the latest, cutting-edge tech and thought it would be nice to be ready for Wifi 6 for when I eventually get an iPhone 11 or some other device that features that protocol. But unfortunately, the negative experiences do not come only when I look at the thing.

I was at first alarmed, as I set up the router, by what a very long time it took anything to happen in the app. At every point at which I so much as switched to a different screen in the app, both during and after setup, the app would chug for an alarmingly long time before finally displaying the page I'd navigated to. This is to be expected when the router needs to restart, but...these were not points at which the router needed to restart. These were not points at which I'd changed any setting at all. These were points at which nothing at all had happened except that I'd attempted to go from, say, the app's main page to the Device Manager page, or the Wifi Settings page, or wherever. Simply switching pages in the app would take 20 or 30 seconds or longer. Another negative first impression.

I also noticed that the app doesn't give me access to a lot of the features of the router I expect to have access to. Granted, I'm an advanced user compared to a lot of people - networking is an aspect of computing I've enjoyed mucking around in for decades now, and my inclination with a new router (or an old one, for that matter) is to dive straight into areas of the settings where many ordinary users may fear to tread. But the Nighthawk phone app appears to be targeted more toward the average consumer. Which, if you're more the average consumer, is fine. But if you're me, you find that to be a disappointing restriction.

Then I started trying to use the web UI instead, and while it gave me access to all those more techy parameters I sought, I found the same delay problem happening when I tried to switch from one page of settings to another, but here it happened for longer, and sometimes the target page wouldn't load at all until I clicked again, this time on the blank page with the spinning progress indicator in the center.

So both of the means I have for interfacing with the router are inordinately slow, and one of them is clunky and glitchy on top of it.

And finally, add to all this the way I will occasionally go to navigate to any ordinary webpage and be told my browser can't display the page because I'M NOT CONNECTED TO THE INTERNET, and voila! - the straw that broke the proverbial camel's back.

This happens, and I go and look at the router to see if maybe it's restarted itself for some reason (automatic software update?) and...no. All lights are on and looking as they do during normal operation; the router's just not providing said normal operation.

I never once had such problems with the Apple AirPort Extreme I replaced with this router, nor with the Linksys AC5400 I bought more recently and then wound up giving to a friend. So, because I want a router that, unlike the AirPort Extreme, is tri-band, is still supported with software/firmware updates, and might also feature better performance with multiple connected devices, I bought myself another AC5400 with which I will be replacing this unsatisfactory Netgear thing as soon as it arrives.

And also because I decided I can wait for Wifi 6 until such time as I actually do have devices capable of taking advantage of it, which may be quite some time (i just bought a new MacBook Pro which doesn't support it, and I don't see the iPhone 11 as having any compelling advantages over my iPhone XS Max, soooo...).

The Linksys AC5400 is a monster among 802.11ac routers and has garnered much respect in tech mags and blogs and so forth. Plus I myself have about a year's experience with one and it's been fast, reliable, and glitch-free. So if you're looking for a new router and don't feel compelled to buy into 802.11ax just yet (few devices support it yet anyways), I heartily recommend that one.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Nighthawk 4-Stream AX4 Wi-fi 6 Router (RAX40) – AX3000 Wireless Speed (Up to 3 Gbps) | 1,500 Sq Ft Coverage

text_fidelity_a:
Polaroid Cube HD 1080p Lifestyle Action Video Camera (Black) [Discontinued by Manufacturer] I was rather surprised when I got this with how small it is. I knew from the product description that it would be a little guy, but didn't have an appreciation for how small it was until I got it. It's a cube that is less than 1.5 inches on each side. Very compact, but it feels very solid and well-made.

Despite the compact size this is a solid performer. The video quality is quite clear and vivid provided you keep the cam steady. That's not easy to do if this is handheld given the small size, but it's designed to be mounted (there's a magnet in the base plus there are a variety of options available for mounting. Note that the mounts are sold separately).

The sound quality is good. Not spectacular, but reasonably clear and on a par with most cams I've used that have an internal mic.

Getting to the SD card is where the small size does cause a problem - it's not all that easy if you don't have nimble fingers (which I do not). You need to open the access door (which is sealed for water resistance) with a coin.

It doesn't have a lot of features which I find to be a plus since it greatly simplifies operation - the interface is a single button that turns it on/off, takes a still or starts/stops video recording. Can't get easier than that!

Minor quibbles aside, this is a solid performer and one that's well worth considering if you're looking for a very unobtrusive cam that's easy to operate (other than getting the SD card in and out). 4.5 stars rounded up to 5 due to the performance at this price point.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Polaroid Cube HD 1080p Lifestyle Action Video Camera (Black) [Discontinued by Manufacturer]

text_fidelity_a:
ViewSonic VA2359-SMH 23 Inch IPS 1080p LED Monitor with HDMI and VGA Inputs What I like about this monitor:
1. Easy to set up - I used my previous monitor video cable and power cord and had it up and running in a few minutes.
2. Very clear resolution despite having an old video card.
3. It has an HDMI connection but I am using the regular VGA input and it still very clear.
4. A VGA and sound cord are included.
5. Very sleek, streamline black design which goes nicely with my other computer accessories.

What could be better:
1. The included instructions tell you nothing about how to make video and audio adjustments. I can't use a bright setting and it took a good while to figure out how to use the buttons underneath the screen. They are not intuitive at all.
2. Poor Audio - if you want good audio from this monitor that will not be possible. It is a thin monitor and the audio is very thin and tinny. I was hoping I could disconnect my external sound system to make more room on my desk but found out that I must keep it if I want to hear any decent sound from my computer.
3. While testing the volume on this monitor you must still figure out how to toggle using the various buttons underneath. There is no single volume button or toggle switch. And it will not get very loud.
4. If you don't bump the monitor or use the toggle switches the monitor stays fairly steady on it's stand. Otherwise it will rock and jiggle while using the buttons.
5. No HDMI cable is included.

The scant instructions did say to visit their website to download the latest drivers but as of yet this monitor is not listed in their driver drop down window. I don't think that matter much at this time as the monitor is very clear and sharp.
Overall: Good monitor for the price (as of this review it costs $138.24 Prime) which I feel is a fair price.
text_fidelity_b: ViewSonic VA2359-SMH 23 Inch IPS 1080p LED Monitor with HDMI and VGA Inputs

text_fidelity_a:
Sony A90J 65 Inch TV: BRAVIA XR OLED 4K Ultra HD Smart Google TV with Dolby Vision HDR and Alexa Compatibility XR65A90J- 2021 Model The box took a big gouge in shipping (in just the original TV box), but the TV was fine, so packaging is probably adequate. Unboxing was easy and there was just a bit of styrofoam and minimal cardboard. Be careful with removing the television from the box, because these things are getting thin enough to be bent under their own weight.

It mounted fine on my old wall mount, but required a different screw size. The screws from my previous setup were the wrong size, so you might want to check what you've got and order some so you don't have to wait around.

There isn't much thought put into cable management, so you'll have to come up with your own solution if you don't want cords visible. Power cord is in the lower right quadrant. Most of the other cords are in the lower left, as is a well hidden power button on the back left. The instructions are minimal. I tried hooking my receiver in as instructed to use the television speaker in place of my old center speaker, but it wouldn't work. It may have just been a clash of brands and standards, because every time I tried to switch to using the TV speakers in the options, it would shut off my Pioneer receiver instead. I ended up using the other speaker input, which did work. I can't believe we're in the 2020's and still cramming bare wires in as audio input. I've got a drawer full of various audio cables here.

Turning it on, I was greeted with setup options. The remote seems high quality, but I wish it had some air-remote functionality. Navigating menus with buttons can get a bit confusing. After getting it hooked up to wifi, I was off to YouTube to find something to make sure it was working right before I hooked everything else up. One of those HD coral reef relaxation videos was just the thing. The picture is vibrant! Bright and colorful. The bezels aren't small enough to tile these together, but are very small. My kids wouldn't let me change the video for hours. They just sat and watched the fish. I'm susceptible to the whine some televisions put out, and I've heard none of that. Worked great for video games, though I didn't try anything especially high end. Worked well for computer output. With the exception of that one audio jack compatibility issue, and the different sized screws, everything has worked as expected.

The screen is a speaker, like a modern smartphone. Sound is good, especially at frequencies you would hear from a center speaker. I definitely still wanted my subwoofer and side speakers to round things out, but it's really nice to have the voices from the television coming from where the faces are, not from some speaker below the television.

I don't have a different brand of 2021 television to compare it to, but my impression is that there is a bit of a premium for the brand name, but it's a very nice product. This was certainly an upgrade for me. A lot of progress has been made in the 8 years since I last upgraded.
text_fidelity_b: Sony A90J 65 Inch TV: BRAVIA XR OLED 4K Ultra HD Smart Google TV with Dolby Vision HDR and Alexa Compatibility XR65A90J- 2021 Model
